spans.content: Catalytic Aerobic Oxidation of p-Methoxybenzyl (PMB)
Ethers to Aldehydes or Ketones
Qian Zhang,[a] Hui Qian,*[a] and Shengming Ma*[a, b]
An efficient and highly selective aerobic oxidation of p-
methoxybenzyl ethers to aldehydes or ketones with Fe-
(NO3)3 · 9H2O and TEMPO as catalysts at
2 5 ^ { \circ } C
has been
developed. This method is compatible with versatile functional
groups: adamantyl, ether, alkynyl, and alkenyl, etc. Due to the
mild nature of the reaction conditions, even the highly sensitive
optically active aldehydes with an easily racemized α-chiral
center could be formed from optically active PMB ethers
without racemization. Other protecting groups of hydroxyl
group remained intact during the current aerobic oxidation.
The catalytic protocol has been successfully applied to synthesis
of (R)-tert-butyldimethylsilyl hept-1-en-6-yn-4-yl ether, which is
the key intermediate for the total synthesis of natural product,
(� )-6-O-methylcitreoisocoumarin.

solution.

Results and Discussion
When using Fe(NO ) · 9H O and TEMPO as catalysts,[5] the
reaction of PMB ether of dodecanol 1 a in toluene was very
slow (Table 1, entry 1). With 6 mol % KCl as the additive, the
reaction rate was slightly increased (Table 1, entry 1 vs. entry 2).
Further increasing the amount of KCl to 12 mol% led to 74%
NMR yield of aldehyde 2 a and 18 % NMR yield of carboxylic
acid 3 a (Table 1, entry 3). Surprisingly, upon increasing KCl to
18 mol%, 71% NMR yield of dodecanal 2a was obtained with
an exclusive selectivity for the formation of aldehyde 2 a over
carboxylic acid 3 a, although 9 % recovery of PMB ether 1 a
remained. In addition, nitrite
{ \pmb { 1 } } \mathbf { a } ^ { \prime \prime }
was also formed (Table 1,
entry 4). There is a striking solvent effect since the reaction in
DCM or MeCN afforded carboxylic acid 3 a as the major product
(Table 1, entries 5 and 6). When MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether)
was applied as the solvent, the selectivity is poor forming a
mixture of 30% NMR yield of aldehyde 2 a, 16 % NMR yield of
carboxylic acid 3 a, 22 % of alcohol 1 a’, and 23 % recovery of 1 a
(Table 1, entry 7). The reaction with
\mathsf { C u } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } \cdot 3 \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
replacing
\mathsf { F e } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } \cdot \mathsf { 9 H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
was much slower (Table 1, entry 8). In the
absence of
\mathsf { F e } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } \cdot \mathsf { 9 H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
or TEMPO, no reaction occurred
(Table 1, entries 9 and 10). We also found that pre-stirring of the
catalysts was beneficial for the reaction (Table 1, entry 4 vs.
entry 11). If the catalysts had not been pre-stirred before adding
PMB ether, 66 % NMR yield of aldehyde 2 a and 13 % recovery
of 1 a were detected within the same reaction time (Table 1,
entry 11).

(NO3)3 · 9H2O/TEMPO-cocatalyzed aerobic oxidative reaction. As
shown in Scheme 2, PMB ether with alkyl chain length of 12
carbon atoms gave dodecanal 2 a in 82% yield. When the
length of alkyl chain was increased to 18, the reaction may also

substrate with a highly sterically hindered group such as
adamantyl also worked affording aldehyde 2 c. Interestingly,

remained. In addition, nitrite
{ \pmb { 1 } } \mathbf { a } ^ { \prime \prime }
was also formed (Table 1,
entry 4). There is a striking solvent effect since the reaction in
DCM or MeCN afforded carboxylic acid 3 a as the major product
(Table 1, entries 5 and 6). When MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether)
was applied as the solvent, the selectivity is poor forming a
mixture of 30% NMR yield of aldehyde 2 a, 16 % NMR yield of

(Table 1, entry 7). The reaction with
\mathsf { C u } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } \cdot 3 \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
replacing
\mathsf { F e } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } \cdot \mathsf { 9 H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
was much slower (Table 1, entry 8). In the
absence of
\mathsf { F e } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } \cdot \mathsf { 9 H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
or TEMPO, no reaction occurred
(Table 1, entries 9 and 10). We also found that pre-stirring of the

of 1 a were detected within the same reaction time (Table 1,
entry 11).

(NO3)3 · 9H2O/TEMPO-cocatalyzed aerobic oxidative reaction. As
shown in Scheme 2, PMB ether with alkyl chain length of 12
carbon atoms gave dodecanal 2 a in 82% yield. When the
length of alkyl chain was increased to 18, the reaction may also
proceed smoothly to afford octadecanal 2 b in 75 % yield. The
substrate with a highly sterically hindered group such as
adamantyl also worked affording aldehyde 2 c. Interestingly,
phenyl ether group in 1 d was compatible to give 9-phenox-
ynonanal 2 d in 81% yield. In addition, substrates with terminal/
non-terminal C� C triple bond also proceeded well to afford
targeted aldehydes 2 e–2g in decent yields. PMB ether 1 g
containing a secondary hydroxyl group was successfully
converted to the corresponding aldehyde 2 g with the secon-
dary alcohol unit also being oxidized to ketone. Non-terminal/
terminal C� C double bond, were also compatible to give
corresponding aldehydes (E)-2 h and 2 i. Bis-PMB ether of 1,8-
octanediol 1 j afforded dialdehyde 2 j. Furthermore, the sub-
strates derived from pharmaceuticals and natural products
including ibuprofen, naproxen, flurbiprofen, oxaprozin, dehy-
droabietic acid, and adapalene also run well to give correspond-
ing aldehydes. Notably, the optically active substrates with a
sensitive α-chiral center also worked without racemization
under standard conditions [(S)-2 k and (S)-2 l] due to the mild
nature of the reaction conditions.

We further scrutinized the diol substrate scope of PMB
ethers with different protecting groups of the remaining
hydroxyl group to test the selectivity of this deprotective
oxidation. As shown in Scheme 3, common protecting groups
of hydroxyl group, such as OTBS, OTs, OAc, OBz, and even the
acid-sensitive OMEM group were all compatible (2 q–2 u). When
one of the two hydroxyl groups in 1,6-hexanediol was protected
as PMB ether and the other was protected as p-cyanobenzyl
ether (1v), the PMB ether was highly selectively removed
affording aldehyde 2 v with the p-cyanobenzyl ether remained
untouched. When the secondary hydroxyl group in 1 w was
protected as THP ether, THP group could also be remained.

conditions after 19.5 h (Table 2, entry 1). When using DCE as
solvent, the reaction of 1 y could proceed smoothly to afford
ketone 2 y in 95 % NMR yield (Table 2, entry 2). Control experi-
